newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP to demand ban on abuse of disabled people.
newsitem.headline: EP to demand ban on abuse of disabled people.

text.p: Handicapped people face shocking physical and psychological abuse in the European Union and need legal protection, Euro-MP Mary Banotti told a news conference in the European Parliament on Tuesday.

Voluntary groups representing the EU's 37 million disabled had reported to parliament a catalogue of "abuse and violence against disabled people, especially disabled children in institutional settings," Banotti said.
Pat Matthews from Autistic International told the news conference about little children being forced to eat their own vomit and being hosed down with cold water because they had soiled themselves.
Sexual abuse was widespread, patients were deprived of food and locked up as punishment and "misguided" staff too often used drugs to control their behaviour, Matthews said.
"Children and adults are turned into zombies so they can be contained with the minimum of staff and money," he said.
December 3, designated by the United Nations as the International Day of Disabled People, marks the start of a concerted campaign by Euro-MPs and voluntary groups to criminalise such treatment.
Banotti said she expected to win parliament's support on December 12 for a ban in all EU member states on "the inhumane and degrading treatment of disabled people".

In her report to parliament, published on Tuesday, the Irish Christian Democrat says most handicapped victims are unable to articulate their distress and their parents are often too frightened to complain.
The report highlights the many other ways 10 percent of the EU population are made to feel they are almost sub-human rather than citizens with equal rights.
It urges the EU and the member states to take action, including writing an explicit clause on non-discrimination into the EU treaty.
The humiliation starts with inaccessible buses and polling stations, unusable technology and information.

It extends to unemployment for 70 percent of disabled people and a European single market which promises freedom of movement but where national social security systems are so different as to prevent the disabled moving abroad.
And it cumulates in doctors sterilising the mentally- handicapped or administering electro-convulsive therapy without their consent, the news conference heard.
Parliament is due next week to recommend action on all these levels.
It is also expected to slam Britain and Germany for blocking the extension beyond 1996 of an EU programme to help the disabled.
This will deny voluntary groups 12 million Ecus, in a move heavily criticised by parliament's all-party disability group.
"It is unacceptable that two member states can dictate to the EU in this way and use the disabled as a political football," group chairwoman Barbara Schmidbauer told reporters.
